screens.title: Tools and Techniques for Threat Hunting
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of the toolset and techniques hunters use every day. Good hunting begins with complete, searchable data: logs from endpoints, authentication systems, network flows and packet captures. When those sources are collected and correlated, a hunter can ask focused questions like whether a service account accessed a database at an unexpected hour, or whether a workstation spawned a shell that it never did before. You will learn where to look for that data and how to use SIEM queries, endpoint searches, and network captures to verify and investigate suspicious behavior. We will also cover behavioral analytics and how baselines help prioritize investigations, common operational mistakes that create blind spots, and safe practices for investigating live systems. By the end, you’ll understand the complementary roles of SIEM, EDR, Zeek or packet captures, and NetFlow, and you will be able to pick the right starting point for a hunt. Consider what a single uncollected field — like missing process command-line arguments — does to your ability to prove or disprove a compromise.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Tools and Techniques
Tools and Techniques for Threat Hunting
How SIEM, EDR, network telemetry, and analytics combine to reveal hidden adversary activity.

This chapter shows how hunters move from an alert or hunch to a focused investigation using multiple data layers. You will see example queries and learn when to pivot to endpoint telemetry or packet captures.

In this lesson: technique-driven hunting, verified queries, and safe operational practice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives give a practical target for your hunting skills. First, you will learn to identify and describe the common tools across network, endpoint, and log layers. That includes SIEM platforms for centralized correlation, EDR agents for endpoint visibility, and packet and flow tools for network context. Second, you will demonstrate techniques to query security logs and network data. This means composing focused searches that enrich, filter, and count events so you can spot anomalies. Third, you will explain how EDR enables endpoint-centric hunting: process trees, command-line arguments, memory access, and pivoting from alerts to full endpoint timelines. Finally, you will apply behavioral analytics and anomaly detection to prioritize investigations, understanding baselines and why an out-of-profile action becomes suspicious. Each objective is tied to the ability to ask better questions, reduce blind spots, and produce investigative evidence that supports response decisions.

screens.title: Why Data Visibility Is the Foundation
screens.narratorSegment: Data visibility is the single most important enabler of proactive hunting. When systems forward complete logs to a central platform, you can query across time and correlate events. Important fields include timestamps, user or host identifiers, process names, and command-line arguments on endpoints. Missing command-line details or absent NetFlow metadata will limit your ability to confirm lateral movement or identify exfiltration. Consider a scenario where a suspicious login is reported but the endpoint logs capture no process details: you cannot tell whether that login led to credential dumping or lateral commands. Hunters should therefore verify ingestion pipelines and field mapping as a routine step. Practical checks include making sure SIEM parsers extract source IP, destination host, and user fields, and that EDR captures process parent-child relationships and command-line arguments. A misconception to watch for is assuming that more data is always noise: incomplete data is worse than noisy data because it creates blind spots. The takeaway is clear: before writing hunting queries, ensure the data you need exists and is reliably collected. Why Data Visibility Is the Foundation means verify ingestion and field completeness first; without key fields, focused hunting queries cannot produce reliable evidence.. In practical terms, data completeness, required fields, and the cost of blind spots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Data Visibility
Definition
Data visibility is the degree to which an organization collects, stores, and can search relevant telemetry from endpoints, network devices, and applications.
• Required fields: timestamp, user/host, process name, command line, src/dst IP, port.
• Verify parsers and ingestion pipelines; confirm field extraction in SIEM.
• Check EDR settings for process trees and memory events when investigating fileless techniques.
Concrete Example
A missing command-line field prevents proving that a Microsoft Word document spawned PowerShell with encoded commands. This gap can stop a timely containment action.
Key Takeaway

Confirm the existence and reliability of the fields you will query before starting a hunt.

Checklist for Visibility
1. Ensure SIEM receives authentication and host logs from all critical servers.
2. Confirm EDR agents capture process creation with command-line and parent process fields.
3. Verify NetFlow or Zeek logs are retained long enough to investigate slow exfiltration.
4. Run small test events to validate parser behavior and field extraction.
Common Mistake
Assuming that because a device sends logs, every useful field is present. Fields may be dropped by agents or parsers.

screens.title: Using a SIEM to Query and Enrich Events
screens.narratorSegment: A SIEM is the hunter's central hub for historical analysis and correlation. The typical workflow is: select an index and time window, filter by relevant event types, enrich records with lookups such as geo-IP, and then aggregate to reveal outliers. For example, a query that finds successful Windows logins to critical servers, enriches the source IP with geolocation, filters for non‑local countries, and counts occurrences will quickly surface suspicious access. When you build such queries, keep them as narrow as the hypothesis requires: limit the time window, specify target hosts, and exclude known maintenance accounts. Visualizations help spot trends, but the core value comes from the underlying table of events you can pivot from. A common misconception is to rely on pre-built dashboards alone; dashboards may hide sparse but important events. Practice writing queries that return _time, user, src_ip, dest_host and event_id so the investigation can immediately pivot to endpoint or network data. The next time you see an unusual login, ask: does the SIEM record the full context I need to validate a compromise? Using a SIEM to Query and Enrich Events means build narrow, enriched queries that produce actionable tables you can pivot from to endpoint or packet evidence.. In practical terms, compose focused queries, enrich with lookups, and aggregate to find anomalies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › SIEM Querying
One-sentence subtitle
Compose index, event filters, enrichment lookups, and stats to find anomalous authentications.
Supporting points:
  • Enrich with geoip to detect logins from unexpected countries.
  • Aggregate by user and source IP to count rare occurrences.
  • Keep time windows narrow to reduce noise and speed investigations.
Concrete Example
A Splunk-like query can find successful logins to critical servers, enrich with geoip, filter out the city or country you expect, and count events by user and source IP.
Key Takeaway

SIEM queries should return a compact, pivotable table of events so you can confidently escalate to endpoint or network analysis.

Example Query (Splunk-like)
index=windows_events event_id=4624 (dest_host="critical_server_A" OR dest_host="critical_server_B")
| lookup geoip client_ip AS src_ip
| where geo_country != "United States" AND _time > relative_time(now(), "-7d")
| stats count by _time, user, src_ip, geo_country
| sort - count
This query locates successful Windows logins, enriches source IP with country, filters out expected geography, and returns counts for investigation.
Pitfall
Broad queries over long periods create alert fatigue and hide rare, recent anomalies.

screens.title: Endpoint Detection and Response for Hunting
screens.narratorSegment: EDR solutions give you the finest-grained visibility into what happened on an endpoint. Agents record process creation, parent-child relationships, command-line arguments, module loads, network connections, and sometimes memory access events. These data points let you reconstruct an attack timeline. For example, if a SIEM shows suspicious outbound traffic from a host, an EDR pivot can show the process that initiated the connection, whether a Microsoft Word process spawned PowerShell, and whether that PowerShell instance attempted credential access. A common hunting query looks for instances where a benign process spawns a normally uncommon child, such as winword. exe starting powershell. exe. When writing EDR queries, include time ranges aligned to the SIEM event, filter by host name, and return process_name, parent_process_name, command_line, and user. Beware the misconception that EDR always records everything: agent configuration and retention settings matter. If command-line collection is disabled, you will not see encoded commands. Practice by simulating document-based macro execution and verifying the EDR captures the full command-line and parent process chain. Endpoint Detection and Response for Hunting means use edr to pivot from network or siem alerts to a clear endpoint timeline showing parent-child process relationships and command-line context.. In practical terms, process trees, command-line details, and memory events that reveal attacker behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › EDR Hunting
EDR capabilities
Process creation, parent-child relationships, command-line capture, module loads, network sockets, and memory access events.
Supporting bullets:
  • Pivot from SIEM alerts to endpoint timelines to validate sequences.
  • Look for LOLBINs spawned with unusual arguments or encoded payloads.
  • Prioritize hosts with anomalous behavior flagged by behavioral analytics.
Concrete Example
Search for events where winword.exe spawned powershell.exe; this pattern often indicates a malicious document executing a script.
Key Takeaway

EDR is the source of truth for endpoint behavior. Ensure its collection settings align with your hunting questions.

EDR Query (conceptual)
PROCESS_CREATE where ParentProcessName = "winword.exe" and ProcessName = "powershell.exe"
| select _time, host_name, process_name, parent_process_name, command_line, user
This conceptual query locates instances of a document spawning a shell and returns the command line and user context for investigation.
Misconception
Assuming EDR always retains long timelines by default. Retention and telemetry level are configurable and may be limited.

screens.title: Packet and Flow Tools: When to Use Each
screens.narratorSegment: Network-level hunting requires choosing the right telemetry for the hypothesis. Packet capture tools like tcpdump and Wireshark let you inspect raw packets and payloads, which is essential when you need to identify command-and-control payloads or confirm data exfiltration. Zeek provides high-fidelity, parsed connection-level logs such as DNS requests and HTTP transactions that are easier to search at scale. NetFlow and IPFIX provide conversation metadata — source, destination, ports, byte counts — and are excellent for spotting unusual long-lived low-volume channels that suggest covert C2. The practical trade-offs are storage and fidelity: packets capture everything but are expensive to store; flows are lightweight but lack payloads. A common hunting pattern is to use NetFlow to identify suspicious long-lived connections, pivot to Zeek logs for parsed context, and then collect targeted packet captures for payload inspection. A misconception is treating NetFlow as sufficient to prove protocol misuse; NetFlow tells you that traffic exists and its volume, but you need packets to inspect payloads. Practice combining these sources: flows to triage, Zeek to enrich, packets to confirm. Packet and Flow Tools: When to Use Each means use flow data to detect anomalies, zeek logs for parsed context, and packet captures for definitive payload-level confirmation.. In practical terms, tcpdump/wireshark, zeek, and netflow have different trade-offs for hunting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Network Tools
tcpdump / Wireshark
Full packet capture for payload inspection, protocol decoding, and identifying C2 signatures.
Use when you need to validate payload contents or detect covert channels.
Zeek (Bro)
Parses packets into high-fidelity logs: DNS, HTTP, connections, and file transfers for behavioral hunting.
Use for scalable behavioral searches and forensics without storing full packets.
NetFlow / IPFIX
Lightweight flow metadata for spotting unusual volumes, destinations, and long-lived conversations.
Use to triage and identify hosts needing deeper capture or Zeek parsing.
Example Filter
http.request.method == "POST" and http.request.uri contains "upload"
A Wireshark display filter to look for potential data upload behavior in HTTP traffic.
Key Takeaway

Combine flows, parsed logs, and packets: each layer narrows hypotheses until you can confirm or rule out malicious activity.

screens.title: Baselines and Anomaly Detection in Hunting
screens.narratorSegment: Behavioral analytics help hunters prioritize where to look by flagging deviations from a learned norm. Systems like UEBA or built-in SIEM analytics establish baselines for users and hosts: typical logon times, commonly accessed resources, average data transfer volumes, and usual process families. When a user suddenly logs in from a foreign country and accesses sensitive files they never touched before, the deviation is worthy of investigation even if no malware signature exists. Importantly, an anomaly is an indicator of interest, not proof of compromise. Many false positives come from legitimate changes in work patterns or system upgrades. Effective hunters therefore combine anomaly scores with contextual evidence: is the host patched, what processes ran before the access, and are there concurrent network flows? A misconception is to treat anomaly alerts as binary; instead, treat them as triage signals that guide targeted queries and endpoint pivots. The goal is to reduce time-to-detect by focusing on behavior that deviates from a verified baseline. Baselines and Anomaly Detection in Hunting means anomalies focus your investigation but must be validated with contextual siem and edr evidence before concluding compromise.. In practical terms, how baselining focuses effort and what anomalies really mean. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Behavioral Analytics
What is a baseline?
A statistical model of normal activity for a user or host: logon patterns, typical destinations, and usual process families.
How hunters use it:
  • Prioritize anomalies that deviate strongly from baseline.
  • Correlate anomalies with SIEM events and EDR process histories.
  • Reduce noisy alerts by tuning baselines and exclusion rules for known exceptions.
Concrete Scenario
A user who normally works 9 to 5 logs in at 3 AM from a foreign IP and reads a sensitive database. This sequence is an anomaly that deserves a hunt.
Key Takeaway

Treat anomalies as high-value leads, then validate them with telemetry and context before concluding compromise.

Misconceptions & Guidance
• Anomaly does not equal compromise; investigate context.
• Baselines must be periodically refreshed to reflect legitimate changes in behavior.
• Use anomaly scoring to stack-rank investigations by risk, not to auto-contain without review.
Pro Tip
Enrich anomaly alerts with asset criticality and recent patch status to prioritize human review.

screens.title: Avoiding Common Pitfalls and Refining Queries
screens.narratorSegment: Hunting often fails for operational reasons rather than technical ones. Common pitfalls include incomplete logging, disabled command-line collection on endpoints, and poorly scoped queries that generate too many false positives. To refine your practice, follow a repeatable process: first, validate data availability for the hypothesis; second, narrow the time window and target hosts; third, enrich records with context such as geoip or asset tags; fourth, aggregate by meaningful keys to surface rare behavior; and finally, pivot to EDR or network captures for confirmation. When tuning queries, prefer exclusion lists for known benign activity and test queries on historical data to observe false positive rates. Alert fatigue arises when generic rules fire constantly; reduce it by making rules dependent on multiple signals or requiring higher anomaly scores. A misconception to correct is believing broader coverage catches more threats; in reality, targeted, enriched searches combined with good visibility produce faster, more reliable detections. Practice refining a query iteratively until its signal-to-noise ratio is suitable for human investigators. Avoiding Common Pitfalls and Refining Queries means validate data, narrow scope, enrich results, and iterate queries to increase signal and reduce fatigue.. Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Lateral Movement Scenario
Scenario
Alert: svc_web_app logged into DB_PROD_01 at 03:00. Normally this account only accesses WEB_APP_01.
Investigative steps:
  1. Run a SIEM query for other logins by svc_web_app in the last 24 hours.
  2. If WEB_APP_01 is the src_host, pivot to EDR on WEB_APP_01 for process creation between 02:50 and 03:10.
  3. Look for suspicious parents or LOLBIN usage and capture command-line details.
Expected Outputs
SIEM: _time, user, src_host, dest_host, event_id. EDR: _time, process_name, command_line, parent_process_name, user.
Check Your Understanding

If EDR shows powershell started by winword on WEB_APP_01 near 3 AM, what would you investigate next? (Hint: credential dumping and network pivots.)

SIEM Query (conceptual)
index=windows_events event_id=4624 user="svc_web_app" dest_host!="WEB_APP_01" _time > relative_time(now(), "-24h")
| table _time, user, src_host, dest_host, event_id
EDR Query (conceptual)
// Conceptual EDR query
host_name="WEB_APP_01" AND event_time BETWEEN "2023-10-26T02:50:00Z" AND "2023-10-26T03:10:00Z" AND
(
  process_name IN ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe", "wmic.exe", "psexec.exe") OR
  command_line CONTAINS "Invoke-Mimikatz" OR
  command_line CONTAINS "net user"
)
| select event_time, process_name, command_line, parent_process_name, user
Run the SIEM query to map scope, then the EDR query to inspect the suspected source host for process activity and command lines.

screens.title: Safety, Privacy, and Operational Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: Hunting involves accessing potentially sensitive user and host data, so safety and privacy considerations are essential. Prefer working on copies of logs or in non-production testbeds whenever possible. When you must interact with live systems, coordinate with change control and system owners and document the exact actions you will take. Make sure that any remote commands or packet captures are authorized and that collection windows are minimized to limit exposure. Be mindful of privacy regulations when analyzing user activity: apply least-privilege access to logs and redact or limit sensitive fields when sharing findings. Another operational constraint is resource impact: live packet captures or heavy EDR queries can degrade system performance. Schedule heavy forensic captures for maintenance windows or use targeted captures limited to specific hosts and time ranges. A common misconception is that hunting always requires intrusive collection. In many cases, well-instrumented logging and retained telemetry enable complete investigations without touching production endpoints. Finally, document every step to preserve chain of custody and to enable reproducible analysis. Safety, Privacy, and Operational Constraints means always prefer non-production analysis, authorize live actions, limit collection scope, and protect privacy while preserving evidence.. In practical terms, how to hunt safely without disrupting production or violating privacy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of the toolset and techniques hunters use every day. Good hunting begins with complete, searchable data: logs from endpoints, authentication systems, network flows and packet captures. When those sources are collected and correlated, a hunter can ask focused questions like whether a service account accessed a database at an unexpected hour, or whether a workstation spawned a shell that it never did before. You will learn where to look for that data and how to use SIEM queries, endpoint searches, and network captures to verify and investigate suspicious behavior. We will also cover behavioral analytics and how baselines help prioritize investigations, common operational mistakes that create blind spots, and safe practices for investigating live systems. By the end, you’ll understand the complementary roles of SIEM, EDR, Zeek or packet captures, and NetFlow, and you will be able to pick the right starting point for a hunt. Consider what a single uncollected field — like missing process command-line arguments — does to your ability to prove or disprove a compromise.

These objectives give a practical target for your hunting skills. First, you will learn to identify and describe the common tools across network, endpoint, and log layers. That includes SIEM platforms for centralized correlation, EDR agents for endpoint visibility, and packet and flow tools for network context. Second, you will demonstrate techniques to query security logs and network data. This means composing focused searches that enrich, filter, and count events so you can spot anomalies. Third, you will explain how EDR enables endpoint-centric hunting: process trees, command-line arguments, memory access, and pivoting from alerts to full endpoint timelines. Finally, you will apply behavioral analytics and anomaly detection to prioritize investigations, understanding baselines and why an out-of-profile action becomes suspicious. Each objective is tied to the ability to ask better questions, reduce blind spots, and produce investigative evidence that supports response decisions.

Now we expand the objectives into practical behaviors you can practice. For tools and data visibility, verify that your SIEM ingests host authentication logs, EDR captures process command lines, and network telemetry includes NetFlow or Zeek logs. A useful mnemonic is 'SEN' — SIEM, Endpoint, Network — to ensure you check all three layers. For querying logs and network data, practice writing focused queries that enrich with lookups and use time windows to reduce noise. Always ask: what fields do I need to prove a claim? For EDR, practice pivoting from a suspicious network alert to a process tree that shows parent and child relationships. Look for living-off-the-land binaries spawning shells. For behavioral analytics, measure baselines before responding. Anomaly flags should drive investigation, not automatic containment without human review. Each card in this screen corresponds to a verified competency milestone for assessing your readiness to hunt.

Data visibility is the single most important enabler of proactive hunting. When systems forward complete logs to a central platform, you can query across time and correlate events. Important fields include timestamps, user or host identifiers, process names, and command-line arguments on endpoints. Missing command-line details or absent NetFlow metadata will limit your ability to confirm lateral movement or identify exfiltration. Consider a scenario where a suspicious login is reported but the endpoint logs capture no process details: you cannot tell whether that login led to credential dumping or lateral commands. Hunters should therefore verify ingestion pipelines and field mapping as a routine step. Practical checks include making sure SIEM parsers extract source IP, destination host, and user fields, and that EDR captures process parent-child relationships and command-line arguments. A misconception to watch for is assuming that more data is always noise: incomplete data is worse than noisy data because it creates blind spots. The takeaway is clear: before writing hunting queries, ensure the data you need exists and is reliably collected. Why Data Visibility Is the Foundation means verify ingestion and field completeness first; without key fields, focused hunting queries cannot produce reliable evidence.. In practical terms, data completeness, required fields, and the cost of blind spots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A SIEM is the hunter's central hub for historical analysis and correlation. The typical workflow is: select an index and time window, filter by relevant event types, enrich records with lookups such as geo-IP, and then aggregate to reveal outliers. For example, a query that finds successful Windows logins to critical servers, enriches the source IP with geolocation, filters for non‑local countries, and counts occurrences will quickly surface suspicious access. When you build such queries, keep them as narrow as the hypothesis requires: limit the time window, specify target hosts, and exclude known maintenance accounts. Visualizations help spot trends, but the core value comes from the underlying table of events you can pivot from. A common misconception is to rely on pre-built dashboards alone; dashboards may hide sparse but important events. Practice writing queries that return _time, user, src_ip, dest_host and event_id so the investigation can immediately pivot to endpoint or network data. The next time you see an unusual login, ask: does the SIEM record the full context I need to validate a compromise? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EDR solutions give you the finest-grained visibility into what happened on an endpoint. Agents record process creation, parent-child relationships, command-line arguments, module loads, network connections, and sometimes memory access events. These data points let you reconstruct an attack timeline. For example, if a SIEM shows suspicious outbound traffic from a host, an EDR pivot can show the process that initiated the connection, whether a Microsoft Word process spawned PowerShell, and whether that PowerShell instance attempted credential access.
